questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: state the controlling idea of a short factual notice
questions.stem: A learner reads a notice of about eighty characters that lists three changes to a bus route, gives one line of reason for each, and closes by saying when the new arrangement begins. Which sentence states the controlling idea of that notice?

options.text: The route is being reorganised from a stated date, and the notice sets out the changes and their reasons
The three changes are listed in the order in which the stations were first opened
options.misconception: invents a chronology the notice never gives

options.text: The notice was written because the number of complaints about the old route has fallen
options.misconception: reverses the trend the notice implies about complaints

options.text: Every passenger who uses the old route will be given a free ticket for the first month
options.misconception: adds a compensation arrangement that appears nowhere in it

questions.explanation: The controlling idea is the sentence that would still be true if every detail but one were cut away, and here that is the sentence about the route being reorganised from a date, with the three changes and the reasons standing as support. The other three are the mistakes a reader makes by latching on to a detail and promoting it. B invents a history the notice does not contain, C turns a complaint situation into a falling one and so invents the reason the notice exists, and D supplies a benefit no part of the text mentions.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence would survive if you deleted every supporting detail from the notice.

Why old radios are harder to repair than modern ones?

options.misconception: requires outside comparison the passage never makes

options.text: What a repair workshop generally charges for its labour?
options.misconception: requires a general rate the passage never states

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: name the tone of a review from the limits it places on its praise
questions.stem: A short review of a new restaurant calls the food plain, praises the service as unusually attentive, and ends by saying the writer will return soon. Which description captures the tone of those sentences?

options.text: Guarded praise, because every compliment is immediately limited by something
Warm enthusiasm, because the writer praises and promises to return
options.misconception: reads the promise to return as praise without noticing the limits

options.text: Cool indifference, because the writer only reports what was observed
options.misconception: reduces a review with a judgement in it to a neutral report

options.text: Open hostility, because the writer sets the restaurant up for a complaint
options.misconception: reads the complaint about the food as the review's overall purpose

questions.explanation: Tone is carried by where the writer puts the pressure, and here every positive word is checked by a negative one: the service is praised only against the plain food, and the promise to return is a qualified one. A detail showing that the library already has a floor where silence is enforced
options.misconception: describes an unrelated part of the building and bears on neither claim

options.text: A detail about how many students use the stairs during the day
options.misconception: counts movement in the building without touching the rooms in question

options.text: A detail about what it costs to replace the library carpet
options.misconception: reports a cost the argument about students never appeals to

questions.learningObjective: infer a text's purpose from the shape in which it is written

options.text: To persuade, and the shape gives it away because the objections are raised and then answered
To inform without taking a side, and the shape gives it away because no view is expressed
options.misconception: misses the fact that the objections are answered rather than merely listed

options.text: To amuse, and the shape gives it away because the rule is described lightly
options.misconception: reads informality as the signal when the shape is argumentative

options.text: To sell something, and the shape gives it away because a price is mentioned
options.misconception: picks up a commercial signal the shape does not contain

questions.explanation: Purpose is easier to read off the shape of a text than off its subject matter, because writers arrange a text to suit the job it has to do. 现在学生的平均睡眠时间比以前短了。 (Students' average sleep is now shorter than before.)
options.misconception: supplies a statistic that supports the claim rather than stating it

options.text: 校车在七点二十分到达。 (The school bus arrives at twenty past seven.)
options.misconception: supplies a timetable fact the claim rests on rather than being the claim

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify the claim that the evidence in a passage does not reach
questions.stem: A passage reports that a village library lends more books each month than it did, that this has happened every year since 2015, and that the building was repainted in 2018. Which claim would a reader NOT be able to support from those facts?

options.text: The rise in borrowing began before the building was repainted
options.misconception: reports a comparison the two dated facts already allow

options.text: More books have been lent each month since 2015 than in the year before
options.misconception: reports a trend the dated figures already establish

options.text: Repainting the building caused the rise in borrowing
The number lent in 2018 was greater than the number lent in 2015
options.misconception: reports a comparison the stated yearly rise already allows

questions.explanation: A passage supports a claim when the facts it reports make the claim likely, and it does not support a claim merely because the claim is about the same topic. Three of these four statements follow: the rise is dated, so it precedes 2018; a rise every year since 2015 means each year exceeded the last; and that includes 2018 over 2015. The repainting is a fact about the same building in the same period, and it is tempting to treat two facts from one building as one cause, but nothing in the passage connects them. Naming that missing link is the whole of the answer.
questions.hint: Ask which statement needs a link between two facts that the passage never supplies.

questions.learningObjective: identify the difference two reports make through word choice alone
questions.stem: Two reports describe the same gathering outside a town hall. One says the demonstrators gathered peacefully; the other says the mob stormed the building. What do those two choices of words do?

The two words are close in meaning, so the reports differ only in the tone of the newspaper
options.misconception: assumes the two words are near-synonyms with one meaning

options.text: Both words are neutral descriptions, so the two reports are equally even-handed
options.misconception: denies that either choice of word loads the sentence

options.text: The second word is the more accurate one, because a crowd may not be called a mob without evidence
options.misconception: treats the loaded word as the more rigorously evidenced one

questions.explanation: Word choice is where a report's lean usually shows, because the events are fixed and the verbs are not. A word for a group acting within the rules sets up a group, and a word for a group acting against them sets up an enemy, and the two sentences then ask the reader for very different verdicts on the same afternoon. The mistake here is to think a strong word is automatically the less accurate one. questions.learningObjective: say what a soft phrase in an official notice is keeping in the background
questions.stem: An official notice says a factory will transfer some staff to other duties rather than saying that posts are being cut. What is the notice doing, and what does the softer wording keep out of view?

options.misconception: replaces a loss with a gain that the notice does not describe

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify the kind of source a fixed four-character expression comes from
questions.stem: A learner meets the fixed expression 亡羊补牢 and asks where it comes from. What kind of source does it have, and what does that tell a reader about how it can be used?

options.text: It comes from an old tale of a herder whose flock was lost and who then repaired the fold the same evening
It is a modern coinage invented for office use and has no earlier history behind it
options.misconception: denies the expression any older source at all

options.text: It comes from a line in a recent newspaper column about repairs to a barn
options.misconception: places the expression in modern writing rather than in an older tale

options.text: It is a rendering of an English proverb about mending a fence
options.misconception: assumes the expression arrived through translation from another language

questions.learningObjective: give the idiomatic reading of a four-character expression rather than its literal one

To add a missing foot to a drawing of a snake

options.misconception: keeps the literal image and reverses the point of the tale

questions.topic: Register and how it is marked
questions.learningObjective: name the technical term for a change of tone and say what marks it
questions.stem: A message to a colleague has been rewritten from a long formal paragraph into three short lines that use contractions and a first-name form of address, and the writer says only that the tone has changed. What is the name for that change, and what marks it?

options.text: Register, marked here by sentence length, contractions and the choice of address form
Style, marked by the choice of typeface in the printed version of the message
options.misconception: confuses register with typography and ignores the wording

options.text: Dialect, marked by the two spellings used for the same word
options.misconception: confuses a choice of tone with a variety of the language

options.text: Genre, marked by the decision to write a note rather than a letter
options.misconception: confuses the level of formality with the kind of document

questions.explanation: Register is the level of formality a speaker or writer adopts for a particular audience, and the marks of it are in the wording: how long the sentences run, whether contractions are used, which form of address is chosen, how much is left unsaid. C confuses tone with variety, and D confuses how formal a document is with what kind of document it is, since a short informal note and a short formal note are both notes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the change is in the level of formality, the kind of document, or the variety of the language.

questions.learningObjective: say what makes one request formal and another informal
questions.stem: Two requests for the same favour are compared: one says 请您于本周内安排人手处理此事, and the other says 麻烦谁有空帮忙弄一下. What distinguishes them?

The first is polite and the second is rude, although both are equally formal in register
options.misconception: reads informality as rudeness and ignores the shared politeness

options.text: The first is written and the second is spoken, although either could appear in writing
options.misconception: confuses the level of formality with the medium of writing

options.text: The first commands and the second requests, although both are asking for the same help
options.misconception: reads a request for action as an order given

C and D are both right about form and wrong about what the difference means.
questions.hint: Ask how far each version puts between the writer and the person being asked.

questions.learningObjective: judge whether a repetition in a translation is an error or part of the idiom
questions.stem: A translator leaves a phrase containing 的时候 as the English at the time when, and a reviewer marks it as needless repetition. What is the right verdict on the reviewer's objection?

The repetition is an error by the translator and should be removed in every single case
options.misconception: believes no repetition in this language can ever be deliberate

options.text: The repetition marks emphasis and the translator should have doubled it a second time
options.misconception: reads a neutral marker as a device for pressing a point

options.text: The repetition shows that the sentence being translated was poorly written to begin with
options.misconception: blames the source text for a feature of the target language

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: say what the presence of a regional measure word shows about the language
questions.stem: A dictionary lists a general measure word and then records that one area uses a different measure word for the same kind of object. What does the regional entry show about the language rather than about the standard?

options.text: It shows that the spoken varieties differ in grammar, not only in which words they have chosen
It shows that the regional word is a mistake that any speaker will correct on being told
options.misconception: treats a variety feature as an error to be corrected

options.text: It shows that the two areas count objects in fundamentally different ways
options.misconception: overstates a difference in one word into a different counting system

options.text: It shows that the general word was invented by teachers rather than by speakers
options.misconception: attributes the general word to schooling without evidence

questions.explanation: The interesting part of a regional entry is what class of thing it belongs to. If the only difference between two areas were vocabulary, a learner could absorb it as a matter of learning extra words, and a regional measure word is not that: the measure word sits in the grammar, in a slot the language requires, and the two areas fill that slot differently. So the entry is evidence that a variety can differ structurally, which is a stronger claim than a difference of vocabulary and one that matters for how a grammar is described. C turns one word into a different counting system, which the entry does not say, and D and B both treat a variety as a defect, which is a judgement rather than a reading.
questions.hint: Ask whether the regional word sits in a grammatical slot or is simply a different vocabulary item.

options.misconception: joins the two clauses in a way that asserts a cause

Which vegetable is meant is unchanged, because the word for the vegetable was not part of what made the original informal; what made it informal was the verb and the noun for the meal. That is the point of doing the rewrite in two steps, since a learner who assumes the informal word is the problem will change the vegetable and preserve the register.

questions.explanation: The two stages test two different things and the pairing is deliberate. Stage one is a claim about what evidence does and does not license, and stage two is a production task that can be checked. Separating them also stops the commonest wrong repair, which is to reach for the more formal word for the vegetable while leaving the sentence just as informal as it was.

Stage two: the rewrite says the firm waited for a lucky result rather than changing its method, and the same judgement survives. What is lost is the picture and the sting: the expression compresses a whole argument about luck and passivity into four characters, and the rewrite has to make that argument in words, so it is longer and blander. It drops the fact that the practice varies by region, so the line will be repeated as if it held everywhere. And it drops the hedges, because a glossary line has no room for what is sometimes done. Every sentence in a text looks equally available, so a reader who has no way of ranking them collects all of them at the same level, and the question about the point then looks like a question about a sentence that is not there. The teaching move that works is to make the point into an object rather than a theme. Ask the learner to write the one sentence they would put at the top of the text, and to write it from memory rather than by copying, and to say which of the details in the text would be pointless if that sentence were false. A detail that would be pointless is not supporting that sentence, and that is a test the learner can run alone. The exercise that trains it without handing over the answer is the following. Give the learner a paragraph and ask for a list of the sentences that could be deleted with no loss to the writer's point. The list is short, it is the same for every reader who has read the text properly, and a learner who deletes the wrong sentences discovers on their own that those sentences were carrying a reason rather than a fact. The feedback to give is not the correct list but the question of what a reader would no longer believe if the deleted sentence were gone.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach a reader to separate what a writer claims from what a writer shows and from what a reader adds
questions.stem: A learner believes everything a text says. Explain how to teach the difference between a claim the text makes, a piece of evidence the text supplies, and an inference the reader adds, and give a way to practise it.

answer.exemplar: Three different things travel under one name in a beginner's reading, and separating them is most of what later work in this unit consists of. A claim is something the text asserts, and it may or may not be true, so the reader's job is to notice that it is asserted rather than to accept it. Evidence is something the text supplies, and the reader's job is to ask what it bears on, because evidence for one claim is often useless for another. An inference is something the reader supplies, and the reader's job is to notice that it is theirs, which is the step a beginner never takes. The teaching that works marks the three differently on the page. Learners underline the claim, box the evidence, and write the inference in brackets, and the reason for the three treatments is that they have different obligations attached. A claim needs corroboration, evidence needs a target, and an inference needs to be declared so that somebody else can check it. The practice that makes the habit stick is the following: give the learner a text and one sentence they are fairly confident about, and ask them to write it as a claim, as an inference, and as something they would need to see in order to believe it. The third of those is the one that teaches the most, because it converts a feeling of understanding into a stated requirement, and a student who can say what would change their mind is a student who can read an argument.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is credited for making the three obligations different rather than for defining the three words, and for giving a practice whose output is a stated requirement rather than a right answer. The item exists because the failure it describes is a habit of credulity that no amount of vocabulary will dislodge.
questions.hint: Ask what obligation each of the three carries, and what a reader would need in order to be wrong about each.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach a learner to diagnose a register problem before rewriting a sentence
questions.stem: A learner rewrites a sentence from a report in a way that is shorter and says exactly the same thing, and an instructor marks it wrong. Explain what the learner has failed to notice, and how to teach the diagnosis so that the failure does not recur.

answer.exemplar: The learner's mistake is a real one and it is very common, because shortening a sentence and keeping its meaning are the two things a beginner is taught to do first. What the learner has not been taught is that a sentence carries a level of formality as well as a content, and that a shorter sentence built from plainer words and shorter connectives is a different kind of sentence, not a tighter version of the same one. A report sentence gains its authority from the words it does not use: named agents, nouns for the actions, a structure the reader can predict, and nothing that depends on a relationship between writer and reader. Take any of those away and the sentence becomes something a colleague might say, which is a different sentence in every respect except its facts. The teaching that works is to make register a separate object before any rewriting happens. Give the learner one sentence and ask them to say who could say it to whom, before asking them to improve it. Then ask them to write a second version for a different audience and to keep the facts identical. The exercise worth running is the reverse one: give two versions that carry the same facts and ask the learner to say which is a document and which is speech, and then to say exactly which words give it away. A learner who can point at the three words responsible has something to hold on to, and one who can only say that the second version sounds more casual will make the same mistake again in a different sentence.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is marked as correct for separating content from register before teaching any technique, and for offering a diagnosis exercise whose output is a set of specific words rather than an impression. The item targets a habit, and the stem describes a learner who is doing everything they were taught and still getting it wrong, which is only possible if the missing thing was never taught.
questions.hint: Ask which words the report sentence uses that the shorter one cannot, and what those words are doing there.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach a writer to make a claim about custom that a reader can check
questions.stem: A student wants to write a short note about how a custom is practised and has written that everybody does it. Explain why that sentence cannot be worked with, what a checkable version must contain, and how to teach the habit to a student who has not done any fieldwork.

answer.exemplar: The sentence fails for a reason worth making explicit, because it is not wrong so much as inert. A claim that everybody does a thing can be neither confirmed nor contradicted, because no observation settles it, so a reader who accepts it has learned nothing and a reader who doubts it has nowhere to push. The two things that make a claim about custom workable are a place and a period, and they do different jobs. The place turns a general statement into a local one that somebody could travel to and check, and it also forces the writer to notice that customs are not spread evenly inside a country, which is usually the surprise in the exercise. The period turns a present-tense statement into a dated one, which is what makes it possible to say whether the custom is still current, is dying out, or has been revived. A checkable version of the student's sentence therefore has a shape: one region named, one practice described concretely enough to be recognised, one statement about how widely it is done now, and one about how it is treated in the city as against the village if the region is large. The teaching for a student with no fieldwork is not to go and find out, which they cannot do yet, but to notice what their sentence lacks. Give them a list of customary sentences in the form everybody does such a thing, ask them to add a region to each, and then ask what would still be uncheckable afterwards. The residue after that exercise is usually a residue of absolutes, and it is worth naming as a category, because everybody, never and always are the words that do the damage.

questions.explanation: This item asks for a teaching explanation and the exemplar is credited for explaining why an inert sentence is worse than a wrong one, for separating what a place does to a claim from what a period does, and for a practice that works without fieldwork. The habit it installs is the one a student can use on a claim they will never be able to check themselves.
questions.hint: Ask what would count against the claim, and then ask which two pieces of information would make it countable.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach a learner to use a fixed expression figuratively and to say when not to use one
questions.stem: A learner translates fixed four-character expressions word for word and produces sentences a speaker finds confusing. Explain what is going wrong, how to test whether an expression is being used correctly, and when a writer is better off without one.

answer.exemplar: What is going wrong is a reading strategy, not a vocabulary gap. A fixed four-character expression is a whole predication: the characters are the remains of a story or a picture, and the sense is what the story or the picture is used to say. A learner who translates the characters has produced a translation of the story, which is grammatical, plausible, and about something else entirely, and a speaker reads it and looks for a second meaning that is not there. The test that fixes this is short and the learner can run it without help. Take the expression and ask whether its subject can be said to be doing what the whole expression describes, not what its characters picture. A firm that waited for a lucky result can be said to be waiting at a tree stump, and a painter who ruined a finished picture can be said to be adding feet to a snake, and both uses are correct; a painter who lost a brush cannot. The second half of the teaching is when not to use one, and that is a register question rather than a correctness question. An expression compresses a whole argument into four characters, which is why writers use them: they are memorable, and they are shared. They are also opaque to anyone who has not met them, and a reader who meets an expression for the first time in a document about a new subject gets a sentence they must stop in. The rule worth teaching is that an expression belongs in a piece whose readers already have the background, and that a document introducing a subject should be written in words the reader can already read. A learner who has both halves stops translating pictures and stops hiding a hard point behind a short phrase.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is credited for treating the error as a reading strategy rather than a vocabulary gap, for giving a test the learner can run unaided, and for making the decision to use an expression a question about the reader rather than about style. The second half is what separates a competent answer from one that only explains the mistake.
questions.hint: Ask whether the subject can be said to be doing what the whole expression describes, and who the reader is.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: teach the moves of a paragraph and a short essay in a way a learner can reuse
questions.stem: A learner can write a correct sentence and cannot organise two of them into a paragraph. Explain the moves a paragraph has to make, how they differ from the moves of a short essay, and how to practise the paragraph before the essay.

answer.exemplar: The reason a learner stalls at two sentences is usually that they are trying to start with the second one. A paragraph has four moves, and they come in an order that cannot be worked out afterwards: say what this paragraph is about, give the reasons, give a second kind of reason, and then say what follows for the reader. The first move is the one a beginner cannot make, because a topic sentence is a claim and a beginner's instinct is to describe, so they write a sentence about a thing rather than a sentence about what is true of it, and no amount of support can attach to that. The teaching move is to make the first sentence arguable. Give the learner a subject and ask for a sentence that somebody could disagree with, and reject every sentence they produce that merely names the subject. Once the first sentence is a claim, the rest of the paragraph has a job, because each support has to bear on it, and the fourth move is available because something has been established. A short essay is the same four moves with two changes: the moves are separated by paragraph rather than by sentence, and there is room for a concession, which means the strongest objection has to be stated fairly and then answered. The reason to practise the paragraph first is that the essay has no new moves in it, only the same moves spread out and with one extra one added, and a learner who cannot hold four moves in a paragraph will lose them in an essay. The exercise that helps is to take a paragraph a learner has written and label each sentence with the move it was trying to make, including any sentence that was making none.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is credited for making the first move a claim rather than a description, for showing that the essay's moves are the paragraph's moves plus one, and for a labelling exercise that works on the learner's own text. The item is worth asking as a single explanation because the structure is reusable, and a learner who has the moves can build almost any short piece from them.
questions.hint: Ask what the first sentence must be capable of, and what the rest of the paragraph is then for.
